f: Who is the author of the poetic rendition (manẓūmah) of the Ājurrūmiyyah?
b: Ibn Ābb (ابْنُ آبٍ), whose name is Muḥammad.

f: What is the purpose of Ibn Ābb's poetic rendition of the Ājurrūmiyyah?
b: To make Ibn Ājurrūm's prose text easier to memorize by putting it into verse.

f: For whom did Ibn Ābb compose this poem?
b: For anyone who wishes to memorize the Ājurrūmiyyah but finds memorizing its prose difficult.

f: How is kalām (الْكَلَامِ) defined in Arabic grammar according to the Ājurrūmiyyah?
b: Kalām is a spoken expression (لَفْظٌ) that is composed (مُرَكَّبٌ), conveys a complete meaning (مُفِيدٌ), and has been assigned by convention (مَوْضُوعٌ).

f: Into what three categories is kalām divided in Arabic grammar?
b: Kalām consists of three categories: noun (اِسْم), verb (فِعْلِ), and particle (حَرْف).

f: By what signs is a noun (اسْمٌ) recognized in Arabic grammar?
b: A noun is recognized by accepting kasrah (الْخَفْضُ/الْجَرُّ), tanwīn, the definite article الْ, or a preposition (حَرْفُ جَرِّ) before it.

f: Which prepositions (حُرُوفُ الْجَرِّ) are mentioned in the Ājurrūmiyyah?
b: مَنْ، إلَى، عَنْ، فِي، رَبِّ، الْبَاءِ، عَلَى، الْكَافِ، اللَّامُ، الْوَاوُ، التَّاءُ، مُذْ، مُنْذُ، لَعَلَّ، حَتَّى.

f: By what signs is a verb (فَعَلَ) recognized in Arabic grammar?
b: A verb is recognized by accepting سُ, سَوْفَ, قَدْ, or the feminine tāʾ (تَاءُ التَّأْنِيثُ السَّاكِنَةُ).

f: By what sign is a particle (حَرْف) recognized in Arabic grammar?
b: A particle is recognized by not accepting any of the signs of a noun or a verb.

f: What is the role of the word بَلَى in the discussion of particles?
b: بَلَى is given as an example of a particle (حَرْف).

f: How is iʿrāb (الْإِعْرَابِ) defined in Arabic grammar?
b: Iʿrāb is the change in the endings of words, whether expressed explicitly (لَفْظًا) or understood implicitly (تَقْدِيرًا).

f: What causes the changes of iʿrāb in Arabic grammar?
b: The changes are caused by different governing agents (الْعَوَامِل) that affect the words.

f: What are the four categories of iʿrāb?
b: Rafʿ (رَفْعُ), Naṣb (نَصْبِ), Khafḍ/Jarr (خَفْضِ/جَرٍّ), and Jazm (جَزْمٍ).

f: Which parts of speech can have rafʿ (رَفْع) and naṣb (نَصْبٍ)?
b: Both nouns (الْأَسْمَاءُ) and the present tense verb (الْفِعْلُ الْمُضَارِعُ) can have rafʿ and naṣb.

f: Which part of speech is uniquely characterized by khafḍ/jarr (الْخَفْضُ/الْجَرُّ)?
b: Nouns (الْأَسْمَاءُ) alone are characterized by khafḍ (jarr).

f: Which part of speech is uniquely characterized by jazm (الْجَزْمُ)?
b: The present tense verb (الْفِعْلُ الْمُضَارِعُ) alone is characterized by jazm.

f: What are the signs of rafʿ (رَفَعَ) in Arabic grammar?
b: The signs of rafʿ are ḍammah (الضِّمَّةُ), wāw (الْوَاوُ), alif (الْأَلْفُ), and nūn (النُّونُ).

f: When is the ḍammah (الضَّمَّةِ) the sign of rafʿ?
b: It is the sign of rafʿ for the singular noun (الِاسْمُ الْمُفْرَدُ), the broken plural (جَمْعُ التَّكْسِيرِ), the sound feminine plural (جَمْعُ الْمُؤَنَّثِ السَّالِمِ), and the present tense verb (الْفِعْلُ الْمُضَارِعُ) that is not attached to anything affecting its ending.

f: Give examples of nouns that are raised with a ḍammah.
b: جَاءَ زَيْدٌ (singular noun), a broken plural, and a sound feminine plural are all raised with a ḍammah.

f: When is the wāw (الْوَاوُ) the sign of rafʿ?
b: It is the sign of rafʿ for the Five Nouns (الْأَسْمَاءُ الْخَمْسَةُ) and the sound masculine plural (جَمْعُ الْمُذَكَّرِ السَّالِمِ).

f: What are the Five Nouns (الْأَسْمَاءُ الْخَمْسَةُ)?
b: أَبِ، أَخِ، حُمّ، فَو، ذُو (when they meet the conditions for being treated as the Five Nouns).

f: When is the alif (الْأَلْفِ) the sign of rafʿ?
b: It is the sign of rafʿ for the dual (الْمُثَنَّى).

f: When is the nūn (النُّونُ) the sign of rafʿ?
b: It is the sign of rafʿ for the Five Verbs (الْأَفْعَالُ الْخَمْسَةُ).

f: What are the Five Verbs (الْأَفْعَالُ الْخَمْسَةُ)?
b: The present tense forms يَفْعَلَانِ، يَفْعَلُونَ، تَفْعَلَانِ، تَفْعَلِينَ، تَفْعَلُونَ.

f: What are the signs of naṣb (النَّصْبُ) in Arabic grammar?
b: The signs of naṣb are fatḥah (الْفَتْحَةُ), alif (الْأَلِفُ), kasrah (الْكَسْرَةُ), yāʾ (الْيَاءُ), and the omission of the nūn (حَذْفُ النُّونِ).

f: When is the fatḥah (الْفَتْحَةِ) the sign of naṣb?
b: It is the sign of naṣb for the singular noun (الِاسْمُ الْمُفْرَدُ), the broken plural (جَمْعُ التَّكْسِيرِ), and the present tense verb (الْفِعْلُ الْمُضَارِعُ).

f: When is the alif (الْأَلْفِ) the sign of naṣb?
b: It is the sign of naṣb for the Five Nouns (الْأَسْمَاءُ الْخَمْسَةُ).

f: When is the kasrah (الْكِسْرَةُ) the sign of naṣb?
b: It is the sign of naṣb for the sound feminine plural (جَمْعُ الْمُؤَنَّثِ السَّالِمِ).

f: When is the yāʾ (الْيَاءِ) the sign of naṣb?
b: It is the sign of naṣb for the dual (الْمُثَنَّى) and the sound masculine plural (جَمْعُ الْمُذَكَّرِ السَّالِمِ).

f: When is the omission of the nūn (حَذْفُ النُّونِ) the sign of naṣb?
b: It is the sign of naṣb for the Five Verbs (الْأَفْعَالُ الْخَمْسَةُ).

f: What are the signs of khafḍ/jarr (الْخَفْضُ/الْجَرُّ) in Arabic grammar?
b: The signs of khafḍ are kasrah (الْكَسْرَةُ), yāʾ (الْيَاءُ), and fatḥah (الْفَتْحَةُ).

f: When is the kasrah (الْكِسْرَةُ) the sign of khafḍ?
b: It is the sign of khafḍ for the singular noun (الِاسْمُ الْمُفْرَدُ), the fully declinable broken plural (جَمْعُ التَّكْسِيرِ الْمُنْصَرِفُ), and the sound feminine plural (جَمْعُ الْمُؤَنَّثِ السَّالِمِ).

f: When is the yāʾ (الْيَاءِ) the sign of khafḍ?
b: It is the sign of khafḍ for the dual (الْمُثَنَّى), the sound masculine plural (جَمْعُ الْمُذَكَّرِ السَّالِمِ), and the Five Nouns (الْأَسْمَاءَ الْخَمْسَةَ).

f: When is the fatḥah (الْفَتْحَةِ) the sign of khafḍ?
b: It is the sign of khafḍ for every diptote (الِاسْمُ الَّذِي لَا يَنْصَرِفُ).

f: What are the signs of jazm (الْجَزْمُ) in Arabic grammar?
b: The signs of jazm are sukūn (السُّكُونُ) and omission (الْحَذْفُ).

f: When is sukūn (السُّكُونِ) the sign of jazm?
b: It is the sign of jazm for a present tense verb whose final letter is sound (الْفِعْلَ الْمُضَارِعَ الصَّحِيحَ الْآخَرَ), such as لَمْ يَقُمْ.

f: When is omission (الْحَذَفِ) the sign of jazm?
b: It is the sign of jazm for present tense verbs ending in a weak letter (الْمُعْتَلُّ الْآخَرُ) and for the Five Verbs (الْأَفْعَالُ الْخَمْسَةُ).

f: Into how many categories are verbs divided in Arabic grammar?
b: Verbs are divided into three categories: the past tense (الْفِعْلُ الْمَاضِي), the imperative (فِعْلُ الْأَمْرِ), and the present tense (الْفِعْلُ الْمُضَارِعُ).

f: What is the normal ending of the past tense verb (الْفِعْلُ الْمَاضِي)?
b: The past tense verb is always built on fatḥah at its end (مَفْتُوحَ الْآخِرِ), as a general rule.

f: What is the grammatical state of the imperative verb (فِعْلُ الْأَمْرِ) according to the Ājurrūmiyyah?
b: The poem states that, according to some grammarians, the imperative is built on what corresponds to jazm (بِالْجَزْمِ).

f: How is the present tense verb (الْفِعْلُ الْمُضَارِعُ) recognized?
b: It is recognized by beginning with one of the letters of نَأَيْتُ (ن، أ، ي، ت).

f: What is the default grammatical ruling of the present tense verb (الْفِعْلُ الْمُضَارِعُ)?
b: Its default ruling is rafʿ (رَفَعَ) when it is not preceded by a naṣib (particle causing naṣb) or a jāzim (particle causing jazm).

f: Which particles cause the present tense verb (الْفِعْلُ الْمُضَارِعُ) to be in the naṣb state?
b: The naṣib particles are أَنَّ، لَنْ، إذَنْ، كَيْ، لَامَ كَيْ، لَامَ الْجُحُودِ، حَتَّى, and the verb is also put into naṣb after the fāʾ of causation (فَاءَ السَّبَبِيَّةِ), the wāw of accompaniment (وَاوُ الْمَعِيَّةِ), and أَوْ in the appropriate constructions.

f: Which particles cause the present tense verb (الْفِعْلُ الْمُضَارِعُ) to be in the jazm state?
b: They are لَمْ، لَمَّا، أَلَمْ، أَلَمَّا، لَامَ الْأَمْرِ، لَامَ الدُّعَاءِ، لَا النَّاهِيَةُ، لَا الدُّعَائِيَّةُ, and the conditional particles إنَّ، مَا، مِنْ، أَنَّى، مَهْمَا، أَيْ، مَتَى، أَيَّانِ، أَيْنَ، إذْمَا، حَيْثُمَا، كَيْفَمَا, and إذَا when used in poetry (not prose).

f: In what context does إِذَا function as a particle causing jazm?
b: It causes jazm only in poetry, not in normal prose.

f: What is a fāʿil (فَاعِلٌ) in Arabic grammar?
b: A fāʿil is the noun to which an action is attributed; it is the doer of the verb and is in the rafʿ state.

f: Can the fāʿil be explicit or implicit?
b: Yes. It may be an explicit noun (ظَاهِرُ) or an implicit pronoun (ضَمِيرِ).

f: Why might the fāʿil (subject) be omitted from a sentence?
b: It may be omitted for brevity, because it is unknown, or because the speaker wishes to leave it unspecified.

f: What happens to the direct object (الْمَفْعُولِ بِهِ) when the fāʿil is omitted?
b: It takes the place of the subject, becomes the deputy subject (نَائِبُ الْفَاعِلِ), and is put in the rafʿ state.

f: How is the past tense verb changed when forming the passive voice?
b: The first letter is given a ḍammah, and the letter before the last is given a kasrah.

f: How is the present tense verb changed when forming the passive voice?
b: The first letter is given a ḍammah, and the letter before the last is given a fatḥah.

f: Can the deputy subject (نَائِبُ الْفَاعِلِ) be explicit or implicit?
b: Yes. Like the fāʿil, it may be an explicit noun or an implicit pronoun.

f: What is a mubtadaʾ (الْمُبْتَدَأ) in Arabic grammar?
b: A mubtadaʾ is a noun free from any explicit governing agent (عَامِلٌ لَفْظِيٌّ), and it is in the rafʿ state.

f: Can the mubtadaʾ (الْمُبْتَدَأ) be explicit or implicit?
b: Yes. It may be an explicit noun (ظَاهِرُ) or an implicit pronoun (ضَمِيرِ).

f: What is a khabar (الْخَبَرِ) in Arabic grammar?
b: A khabar is the predicate that is ascribed to the mubtadaʾ, and it is always in the rafʿ state.

f: Into what forms can the khabar (الْخَبَرِ) be divided?
b: The khabar may be a single word (مُفْرَدٍ) or a non-single expression (غَيْرِ مُفْرَدٍ).

f: What types of non-single khabar (غَيْرِ الْمُفْرَدِ) are mentioned in the Ājurrūmiyyah?
b: A non-single khabar may be a prepositional phrase (جَارٍ وَمَجْرُورٌ), an adverbial phrase (ظَرْفُ), a verbal sentence (جُمْلَةٍ فِعْلِيَّةٌ), or a nominal sentence (جُمْلَةٌ اسْمِيَّةٌ).

f: What effect do kāna and its sisters (كَانَ وَأَخَوَاتِهَا) have on the mubtadaʾ and khabar?
b: They raise the noun (their subject, اسْمُهَا) and put the predicate (خَبَرُهَا) into the naṣb state.

f: Which verbs are included among kāna and its sisters (كَانَ وَأَخَوَاتِهَا)?
b: كَانَ، أَمْسَى، ظِلٌّ، بَاتَ، أَصْبَحَ، أَضْحَى، صَارَ، لَيْسَ، مَا بَرِحَ، مَا زَالَ، مَا انْفَكَّ، مَا فَتِئَ، مَا دَامَ.

f: What is the ruling for conjugated forms of kāna and its sisters?
b: Any conjugated form of these verbs has the same grammatical effect as the original verb: it raises its noun and puts its predicate into the naṣb state.

f: What effect do inna and its sisters (إِنَّ وَأَخَوَاتهَا) have on the mubtadaʾ and khabar?
b: They put the noun (اسْمُهَا) into the naṣb state and raise the predicate (خَبَرُهَا), which is the opposite of kāna and its sisters.

f: Which particles are included among inna and its sisters (إِنَّ وَأَخَوَاتهَا)?
What is the function of إنَّ (inna)?
b: It is used for emphasis (التَّوْكِيدِ).

f: What is the function of أنَّ (anna)?
b: It is also used for emphasis (التَّوْكِيدِ).

f: What is the function of كأنَّ (kaʾanna)?
b: It is used for comparison or resemblance (التَّشْبِيهِ).

f: What is the function of لكنَّ (lākinna)?
b: It is used for istidrāk (الِاسْتِدْرَاكِ), i.e., introducing a correction or qualification after a previous statement.

f: What is the function of لَيْتَ (layta)?
b: It is used to express wishfulness (التَّمَنِّي).

f: What is the function of لَعَلَّ (laʿalla)?
b: It is used to express hope or expectation (التَّرَجِّي وَالتَّوَقُّعُ).

f: What effect do the verbs of the heart (أَفْعَالُ الْقُلُوبِ) have on a mubtadaʾ and khabar?
b: They make both the original mubtadaʾ and khabar take the naṣb state, turning them into the first and second objects of the verb.

f: Which verbs are listed among the verbs of the heart (أَفْعَالُ الْقُلُوبِ) in the Ājurrūmiyyah?
b: ظَنَّ، وَجَدَ، رَأْى، حَسَبَ، جَعْلَ، زَعَمَ، خَالٍ (خَلْتْ)، اتَّخَذَ، عِلْمٌ.

f: Give an example of a sentence using a verb of the heart.
b: ظَنَنْت زَيْدًا صَادِقًا ("I thought Zayd was truthful"), where both زَيْدًا and صَادِقًا are in the naṣb state.

f: What is a naʿt (النَّعْتِ) in Arabic grammar?
b: A naʿt (adjective) is a follower (تَابِعِ) that describes the noun it modifies (الْمَنْعُوتِ) and follows it in grammatical inflection (iʿrāb).

f: In what does a naʿt (النَّعْتِ) agree with the noun it modifies?
b: It agrees with the manʿūt (الْمَنْعُوتُ) in iʿrāb, definiteness (التَّعْرِيفُ), and indefiniteness (التَّنْكِيرُ).

f: How many categories of definite nouns (الْمَعَارِفِ) are mentioned in the Ājurrūmiyyah?
b: Five categories are mentioned.

f: What are the five categories of definite nouns (الْمَعَارِفِ)?
b: Pronouns (الضَّمَائِرُ), proper nouns (الْأَعْلَامُ), nouns with the definite article "ال", demonstrative nouns (الْأَسْمَاءُ الْمُبْهَمَةُ/أَسْمَاءُ الْإِشَارَةِ), and nouns annexed (مُضَافٌ) to one of these four categories.

f: Which nouns are given as examples of the five categories of definite nouns?
b: أَنَا (pronoun), هِنْدُ (proper noun), الْغُلَامُ (noun with الْ), ذَاكَ (demonstrative noun), and ابْنُ عَمِّنَا (a noun annexed to a definite noun).

f: What is an indefinite noun (النَّكِرَةِ)?
b: An indefinite noun is one that refers to a member of a class without specifying a particular individual.

f: What practical test does the Ājurrūmiyyah give for identifying an indefinite noun (النَّكِرَةِ)?
b: A noun is indefinite if it can validly take the definite article "ال" (e.g., فَرَسُ → الْفَرَسِ, غُلَامُ → الْغُلَامِ).

f: What is ʿaṭf (الْعَطْفِ) in Arabic grammar?
b: ʿAṭf is one of the dependents (التَّوَابِعِ), in which a noun follows another noun through a conjunction.

f: How many conjunctions (حُرُوفِ الْعَطْفِ) are mentioned in the Ājurrūmiyyah?
b: Ten conjunctions are mentioned.

f: Which conjunctions (حُرُوفِ الْعَطْفِ) are listed in the Ājurrūmiyyah?
b: الْوَاوِ، الْفَاءِ، أَوْ، إمَّا، بَلْ، لَكِنْ، حَتَّى، لَا، أُمَّ، الْوَاوُ (The intended list is: الْوَاوُ، الْفَاءُ، ثُمَّ، أَوْ، إمَّا، بَلْ، لَكِنْ، حَتَّى، لَا، أُمَّ; the poem's wording compresses them metrically.)

f: What is the grammatical relationship between a maʿṭūf (conjoined noun) and the maʿṭūf ʿalayh (the noun it follows)?
b: The maʿṭūf follows the maʿṭūf ʿalayh in its grammatical case (iʿrāb).

f: What is tawkīd (التَّوْكِيدِ) in Arabic grammar?
b: Tawkīd is one of the dependents (التَّوَابِعِ) used to emphasize a preceding word.

f: In what does tawkīd (التَّوْكِيدِ) agree with the word it emphasizes?
b: It agrees with the emphasized word in rafʿ, naṣb, khafḍ (jarr), and definiteness.

f: Which words are used for verbal emphasis (التَّوْكِيدُ اللَّفْظِيُّ/الْمَعْنَوِيُّ) according to the Ājurrūmiyyah?
b: النَّفْسُ، الْعَيْنُ، كُلُّ، أَجْمَعَ, along with the words that follow أَجْمَعَ (such as أَجْمَعُونَ، أَجْمَعِينَ, etc.).

f: Give an example of tawkīd using النَّفْسِ.
b: جَاءَ زَيْدٌ نَفْسهُ ("Zayd himself came.").

f: Give an example of tawkīd using كُلِّ.
b: إنَّ قَوْمِي كُلّهُمْ عُدُولٌ ("Indeed, all of my people are upright.").

f: What is badal (الْبَدَلَ) in Arabic grammar?
b: Badal is a dependent (تَابِعٌ) that replaces another noun and takes the same grammatical case (iʿrāb) as the noun it replaces. The poem also notes that a verb may replace another verb.

f: How many types of badal (الْبَدَلَ) are there?
b: There are four types of badal.

f: What are the four types of badal (الْبَدَلَ)?
b: Badal al-kull min al-kull (بَدَلُ الْكُلِّ مِنْ الْكُلِّ), Badal al-baʿḍ min al-kull (بَدَلُ الْبَعْضِ مِنْ الْكُلِّ), Badal al-ishtimāl (بَدَلُ الِاشْتِمَالِ), and Badal al-ghalaṭ (بَدَلُ الْغَلَطِ).

f: What is Badal al-kull min al-kull (بَدَلُ الْكُلِّ مِنْ الْكُلِّ)?
b: It is when the substitute refers to the same entity as the original noun, such as جَاءَ زَيْدٌ أَخُوك ("Your brother, Zayd, came.").

f: What is Badal al-baʿḍ min al-kull (بَدَلُ الْبَعْضِ مِنْ الْكُلِّ)?
b: It is when the substitute refers to a part of the original noun, such as أَكَلْت الرَّغِيفَ نِصْفَهُ ("I ate the loaf—half of it.").

f: What is Badal al-ishtimāl (بَدَلُ الِاشْتِمَالِ)?
b: It is when the substitute refers to something associated with, but not a physical part of, the original noun, such as رَاقَنِي مُحَمَّدٌ جَمَالُهُ ("Muḥammad pleased me—his beauty pleased me.").

f: What is Badal al-ghalaṭ (بَدَلُ الْغَلَطِ)?
b: It is when the speaker corrects a slip of the tongue, such as رَكِبَ زَيْدٌ حِمَارًا فَرَسًا ("Zayd rode a donkey—rather, a horse.").

f: What is a mafʿūl bihi (الْمَفْعُولِ بِهِ) in Arabic grammar?
b: A mafʿūl bihi is the noun upon which the action of the verb falls, and it is in the naṣb state.

f: Can the mafʿūl bihi (الْمَفْعُولِ بِهِ) be explicit or implicit?
b: Yes. It may be an explicit noun (ظَاهِرُ) or an implicit pronoun (ضَمِيرِ).

f: What types of pronouns can serve as a mafʿūl bihi?
b: An implicit object pronoun may be attached (مُتَّصِلٌ) or detached (مُنْفَصِلٌ).

f: What is a mafʿūl muṭlaq (الْمَفْعُولُ الْمُطْلَقُ) in Arabic grammar?
b: A mafʿūl muṭlaq is a verbal noun (maṣdar) in the naṣb state that is used to emphasize, specify, or describe the action of its verb.

f: What is a maṣdar (الْمَصْدَرُ)?
b: A maṣdar is the verbal noun of a verb and is traditionally the third principal form listed in the verb's conjugation.

f: Into what two types is the mafʿūl muṭlaq divided?
b: It is divided into lafẓī (لَفْظِيٌّ) and maʿnawī (مَعْنَوِيٌّ).

f: What is a lafẓī mafʿūl muṭlaq (الْمَفْعُولُ الْمُطْلَقُ اللَّفْظِيُّ)?
b: It is a maṣdar that shares the same root and wording as its governing verb, such as زُرْته زِيَارَةُ ("I visited him with a visit").

f: What is a maʿnawī mafʿūl muṭlaq (الْمَفْعُولُ الْمُطْلَقُ الْمَعْنَوِيُّ)?
b: It is a word that agrees with the meaning of the verb but not its wording, such as فَرُحْت جَذْلًا ("I rejoiced greatly").

f: What is a ẓarf (الظَّرْفِ) in Arabic grammar?
b: A ẓarf is a noun in the naṣb state indicating the time or place of an action, understood with the implied preposition فِي ("in/at").

f: Into what two categories is a ẓarf divided?
b: It is divided into a time adverb (ظَرْفُ زَمَانِ) and a place adverb (ظَرْفُ مَكَان).

f: Give examples of time adverbs (ظُرُوفُ الزَّمَانِ) mentioned in the Ājurrūmiyyah.
b: Examples include الْيَوْمُ، اللَّيْلَةَ، سَحَرًا، غُدْوَةً، بُكْرَةً، غَدًا، حِينًا، وَقْتًا، أَمَدًا، أَبَدًا، عَتَمَةً، مَسَاءَ، صَبَاحَا.

f: Give examples of place adverbs (ظُرُوفُ الْمَكَانِ) mentioned in the Ājurrūmiyyah.
b: Examples include أَمَامَ، قُدَّامِ، خَلْفٍ، وَرَاءَ، فَوْقَ، تَحْتَ، عِنْدَ، مَعَ، إزَاءِ، تِلْقَاءٍ، ثُمَّ، هُنَا، حِذَاءٌ.

f: What is a ḥāl (الْحَالِ) in Arabic grammar?
b: A ḥāl is a noun in the naṣb state that clarifies the condition or state of its possessor (ذُو الْحَالِ) at the time of the action.

f: What is the grammatical case of a ḥāl (الْحَالِ)?
b: A ḥāl is always in the naṣb state.

f: Give an example of a ḥāl (الْحَالِ).
b: Examples include جَاءَ زَيْدٌ ضَاحِكًا ("Zayd came laughing.") and بَاعَ عَمْرٌو الْحِصَانَ مُسْرَجًا ("ʿAmr sold the horse saddled.").

f: What are the grammatical characteristics of a ḥāl (الْحَالِ)?
b: A ḥāl is generally indefinite (نَكِرَةٌ) and supplementary (فَضْلَةٌ), meaning the sentence remains grammatically complete without it.

f: What is the usual grammatical characteristic of the possessor of the ḥāl (ذُو الْحَالِ)?
b: The possessor of the ḥāl is generally definite (مَعْرِفَة) in normal usage.

f: What is a tamyīz (التَّمْيِيِزُ) in Arabic grammar?
b: A tamyīz is a noun that clarifies an ambiguity relating to a preceding word or expression.

f: What is the grammatical case of a tamyīz (التَّمْيِيِزُ)?
b: A tamyīz is in the naṣb state.

f: Give examples of tamyīz (التَّمْيِيِزُ).
b: Examples include طَابَ زَيْدٌ نَفْسًا, لِي عَلَيْهِ أَرْبَعُونَ فَلَسًا, and خَالِدٌ أَكْرَمُ مِنْ عَمْرٍو أَبًا.

f: What is the grammatical characteristic of a tamyīz (التَّمْيِيِزُ)?
b: A tamyīz must be indefinite (نَكِرَة).

f: What are the particles and words of exception (الِاسْتِثْنَاءِ) mentioned in the Ājurrūmiyyah?
b: إلَّا، غَيْرَ، سِوَى، سِوَى، سَوَاءٍ، خَلَا، عَدَا، حَاشَا.

f: What is the ruling of the noun after إلَّا when the sentence is complete and affirmative (تَامَّ مُوجِبِ)?
b: The excluded noun (الْمُسْتَثْنَى) must be in the naṣb state, such as قَامَ الْقَوْمُ إلَّا عُمْرًا.

f: What is the ruling of the noun after إلَّا when the sentence is complete and negative (تَامٌّ مَنْفِيٌّ)?
b: The excluded noun may either be in the naṣb state as a mustathnā or follow the grammatical case of what precedes it as a badal.

f: Give an example of a complete negative exception where both analyses are possible.
b: لَمْ يَقُمْ أَحَدٌ إلَّا صَالِحٌ or لَمْ يَقُمْ أَحَد إلَّا صَالِحًا.

f: What is the ruling of the noun after إلَّا when the sentence is incomplete (اسْتِثْنَاء مُفَرَّغٌ)?
b: It takes whatever grammatical case is required by the sentence structure and is not treated as a normal mustathnā.

f: Give examples of an incomplete (mufarragh) exception.
b: مَا هَدَى إلّا مُحَمَّدٌ (rafʿ), مَا عَبَدْتُ إلّا اللّهَ (naṣb), and هَلْ يَلُوذُ الْعَبْدُ يَوْمَ الْحَشْرِ إلّا بِأَحْمَدَ (jarr after a preposition).

f: What is the grammatical ruling of the noun following غَيْر and سِوَى?
b: The noun following غَيْر and سِوَى is always in the jarr state as a muḍāf ilayh.

f: How are غَيْر and سِوَى themselves declined in a sentence?
b: They take the grammatical case required by their position in the sentence, while the noun after them is in jarr.

f: What is the ruling of the noun after خَلَا، عَدَا، حَاشَا?
b: It may be either naṣb or jarr.

f: Why can the noun after خَلَا، عَدَا، حَاشَا be either naṣb or jarr?
b: If these words are treated as verbs, the following noun is in naṣb; if treated as prepositions, the following noun is in jarr.

f: Give examples showing both rulings after حَاشَا.
b: قَامَ الْقَوْمُ حَاشَا جَعْفَرًا (naṣb) and قَامَ الْقَوْمُ حَاشَا جَعْفَرٍ (jarr).

f: Under what conditions does lā of absolute negation (لَا النَّافِيَةُ لِلْجِنْسِ) put its noun into the naṣb state?
b: When its noun is indefinite (نَكِرَةٌ), directly follows lā without separation, and is singular (مُفْرَدٌ). In this case it is built on fatḥah without tanwīn, e.g. لَا رَيْبٌ.

f: How is the noun after lā of absolute negation (لَا النَّافِيَةُ لِلْجِنْسِ) written when it is a singular indefinite noun?
b: It is without tanwīn and is built on fatḥah, e.g. لَا إِيمَانَ and لَا رَيْبَ.

f: What happens if lā is separated from its noun?
b: Lā must be repeated and is inoperative (مُهْمَلَةٌ), so it no longer governs the noun.

f: What is the ruling when lā is repeated without separation?
b: It is permissible either to make it operative (إعْمَالُهَا) or leave it inoperative (إهْمَالُهَا).

f: Give an example where repeated lā may be operative or inoperative.
b: لَا ضِدَّ لِرَبِّنَا وَلَا نَدَّ (operative) or the second noun may be raised if the second lā is treated as inoperative.

f: How many types of munādā (الْمُنَادَى) are there according to the Ājurrūmiyyah?
b: There are five types.

f: What are the five types of munādā (الْمُنَادَى)?
b: The proper noun (الْمُفْرَدُ الْعِلْمُ), the intended indefinite noun (النَّكِرَةُ الْمَقْصُودَةُ), the unintended indefinite noun (النَّكِرَةُ غَيْرُ الْمَقْصُودَةِ), the annexed noun (الْمُضَافُ), and the noun resembling an annexed noun (الشَّبِيهُ بِالْمُضَافِ).

f: Which types of munādā are built on ḍammah (or its equivalent)?
b: The proper noun (الْمُفْرَدُ الْعِلْمُ) and the intended indefinite noun (النَّكِرَةُ الْمَقْصُودَةُ).

f: Which types of munādā are in the naṣb state?
b: The unintended indefinite noun (النَّكِرَةِ غَيْرُ الْمَقْصُودَةِ), the annexed noun (الْمُضَافُ), and the noun resembling an annexed noun (الشَّبِيهُ بِالْمُضَافِ).

f: Give examples of a munādā built on ḍammah.
b: يَا شَيْخُ and يَا زُهَيْرُ.

f: What is the definition of mafʿūl li-ajlih (الْمَفْعُول لِأَجْلِهِ)?
b: A mafʿūl li-ajlih is a noun in the naṣb state that explains the reason or cause for the occurrence of the action expressed by the verb.

f: Give examples of mafʿūl li-ajlih (الْمَفْعُول لِأَجْلِهِ).
b: قُمْتُ إجْلَالًا لِهَذَا الْحَبْرِ ("I stood out of respect for this scholar.") and زُرْتُ أَحْمَدَ ابْتِغَاءَ الْبِرِّ ("I visited Aḥmad seeking righteousness.").

f: What is the definition of mafʿūl maʿahu (الْمَفْعُولِ مَعَهُ)?
b: A mafʿūl maʿahu is a noun in the naṣb state that comes after the wāw of accompaniment (وَاوُ الْمَعِيَّةِ) to indicate something that accompanies the action.

f: What is the grammatical case of the mafʿūl maʿahu (الْمَفْعُولِ مَعَهُ)?
b: It is always in the naṣb state.

f: After which type of wāw (وَاوٌ) does the mafʿūl maʿahu occur?
b: It occurs after the wāw of accompaniment (وَاوُ الْمَعِيَّةِ).

f: Give examples of mafʿūl maʿahu (الْمَفْعُولِ مَعَهُ).
b: أَتَى الْأَمِيرَ وَالْجَيْشَ ("The commander came along with the army.") and سَارَ زَيْدٌ وَالطَّرِيقَ ("Zayd travelled along the road.").

f: By what means can a noun be in the khafḍ (jarr) state in Arabic grammar?
b: A noun is in the khafḍ state by a preposition (حَرْفُ الْجَرِّ), iḍāfah (الْإِضَافَةُ), or dependency (التَّبَعِيَّةُ) such as naʿt, ʿaṭf, tawkīd, and badal.

f: What is iḍāfah (الْإِضَافَةِ) in Arabic grammar?
b: Iḍāfah is the construction in which one noun (the muḍāf) is annexed to another (the muḍāf ilayh), causing the muḍāf ilayh to be in the jarr state.

f: What is the grammatical case of the muḍāf ilayh (الْمُضَافِ إلَيْهِ)?
b: The muḍāf ilayh is always in the jarr (khafḍ) state.

f: What meanings can an iḍāfah express according to the Ājurrūmiyyah?
b: An iḍāfah may imply لـ (possession or attribution), مَنْ (material or source), or فِي (location or time), depending on the context.

f: Give an example of an iḍāfah implying لـ.
b: ابْنُ أَبِي قُحَافَةَ ("the son of Abū Quḥāfah").

f: Give an example of an iḍāfah implying مِنْ.
b: خَاتَمٌ نُضَارٍ ("a ring of gold").

f: Give an example of an iḍāfah implying فِي.
b: مَكْرُ اللَّيْلِ وَالنَّهَارِ ("the plotting in the night and the day").

f: In which year does Ibn Ābb state that he completed this poetic rendition of the Ājurrūmiyyah?
b: He states that he completed it in the year 1120 AH (عَامِ عِشْرِينَ وَأَلْفٌ وَمِائَةٍ).
